agenticDesign:
RESOLVED POSITION. The three lenses agree on more than they disagree on; I name the five real disagreements and rule on each.

=== A. THE ONE PRINCIPLE ===
Separate the deterministic artifact from the irreversible delivery, and make the artifact a DECLARED OUTPUT. The catalog already contains this shape three times by accident (TsBuild emits dist / NpmPublish ships it; PackageJsonCheck cache:true / PackageJsonWrite cache:false; GithubCiGen contract|check|write). The agentic surveys found it discovered independently three more times (evals/rescore.mjs; alpha-agent-eval-judge.tsx's deterministic scoreTrace as ground truth with the LLM judge scored against it; tevm's pnpm-publish-wrapper splitting pure `pack` from impure `publish` for an unrelated reason and landing on the right seam anyway).

Applied: Agent -> patch.diff (build, verifiable) then AgentApply (run, irreversible). Review -> findings.json (lint) then PublishFindings (run). EvalSample -> retained workspaces (run) then EvalScore (test, cacheable).

=== B. THE HEADLINE FINDING NEITHER SURVEY REPORTED ===
flows has ALREADY SHIPPED a cacheable model-driven target, and it is not LlmLint. It is PackageJson. SyncMode = ["check","write","refresh"] (PackageJson.ts:570, VERIFIED). PackageJsonCheck is kinds:["lint"], cache:true (:1111). PackageJsonWrite is kinds:["run"], cache:false (:1136). The rationale at :882-889: "check and write never call a model. A generated field resolves to the cached model answer for the current input digest; failing that, to the value already on disk; failing that, it is left out entirely. A fresh checkout with a cold cache and no model CLI therefore still checks green, and CI never depends on a network call. Only refresh calls the model, and it is a run target a person invokes."

LlmLint is the OUTLIER, not the template. Its cache:false (VERIFIED at :1344) sits beside a docstring at :1327-1334 that enumerates a complete key — diff content, include and context globs, prompt, rubric, engine, model, model-layer identity, batchSize, failOn. The mechanism was built and then declined. Every new agentic rule copies PackageJson, not LlmLint, and LlmLint is refactored to match.

=== C. DISAGREEMENT 1 — DOES cache:false GET OVERTURNED? ===
Lens A: yes, `nondeterministic: true` already exists in plan/KeyMaterial (VERIFIED at :67, folded at StepKey.ts:391) and Step Keys.md blesses model calls explicitly. Lens B: conditionally, gated on measured verdict-flip rate. Lens C: no — the only cache path is replaying a committed cassette.

RESOLUTION: A is right about JOURNAL REPLAY and wrong about CACHE SHARING; C is right about sharing; B supplies the correct UNIT.
 - Journal replay (resume, fork, time-travel via CacheStore.GetOptions.recordedBy provenance fence) asks "what did this run record", not "what would the model say". It is always correct, needs no new semantics, and agentic targets get it free today. `nondeterministic: true` is exactly right for this and its first-writer-wins conflict semantics.
 - Cross-run cache SHARING requires the model's contribution to be a declared input. `nondeterministic: true` does not make it one. So sharing requires either (i) a committed artifact the target consumes as an input (the patch, the findings, the retained workdir), or (ii) a committed cassette of the model exchange.
 - The UNIT is B's: cache the verdict, not the prose. The gate reads only whether any finding meets failOn (LlmLint.ts:305-306); finding prose will never be byte-stable and nothing gates on it. cache:false currently keys cacheability to the instability of a field nothing consumes.

=== D. DISAGREEMENT 2 — ARTIFACT-RECORD OR TRANSPORT-CASSETTE? ===
They are the same idea at different layers, and they compose. RULING: artifact-level record is the DEFAULT; transport-level cassette is the FALLBACK for outputs that are not human-reviewable. Reasons: a patch.diff or findings.json in a PR is reviewable, portable across model backends, and survives a provider change; a cassette of a codex JSONL stream is none of those, and lens C's own uncertainty flags that it may not be recordable for CLI providers at all. Consequence: Model.Endpoint can carry cassettes because @smthrs/model owns the request bytes (packages/model/src/{RequestExecutor,Protocol,CanonicalJson}.ts exist); claude and codex CLI agents may never be cassette-cacheable, and the catalog must say so rather than imply otherwise.

=== E. DISAGREEMENT 3 — MODEL AS LAYER OR AS ATTR? ===
Both, exactly as Runtime works today. `Runtime.Node({version: ">=22.19.0"})` is an ATTR in BUILD.ts:24 and the resolved runtime is a frozen host-service slot (HostServices.ts:99-105). Model gets the same treatment: the DECLARATION (provider, name, build requirement, decoding params) lands in KeyMaterial.body so it is reviewable in a BUILD diff; the RESOLVED build plus harness digest land in `layers` so a provider ship invalidates. Unanimous across all three lenses: the SEAT/ACCOUNT is NEVER key material. Smithers' agentSig = desc.agent[0].id (engine.js:5558) reordered by live quota headroom plus Date.now is the anti-pattern; alpha-agent-eval-judge.tsx:115-127 already hand-builds an ordered chain in preference to the pool and says why. `models` is an ORDERED NonEmptyArray; the account is recorded in meta for cost attribution only.

=== F. DISAGREEMENT 4 — TTL? ===
Lens A wants TTL scoped to nondeterministic entries; B wants it for verdict-stable targets; C rejects overloading the word "cache". RULING: NO TTL, and this removes a whole mechanism from the build order (VERIFIED: no ttl/expire/freshness anywhere in packages/step-cache). If sharing requires a committed artifact or cassette, the entry IS a pure function of a declared input and a wall-clock expiry would be a lie. "Frozen mediocrity" — a schema-valid but poor answer pinned forever — is handled by the artifact being IN REVIEW (a bad patch.diff shows up in the PR diff) rather than by expiry. This is strictly better than TTL, which would silently re-spend money on a schedule with no human looking.

=== G. DISAGREEMENT 5 — CAN AN AGENT TARGET BE SEALED TODAY? ===
Lens A says sandboxing is THE blocker and proposes it as the decisive experiment. Lens C assumes sandbox: "worktree" works and independently sets tier compensable (for a different reason: two agents racing under one key is how run-hive.sh:77-79 silently reuses someone else's server).

RESOLUTION, and it is the most useful thing here: these reconcile into a shippable wave 1. flows' admission gate is VERIFIED at ActionPersistence.ts:527 — `tier === "sealed" && boundaryMode === "hard" && readsKeyedExactly`. A COMPENSABLE target cannot be cache-admitted AT ALL. So an Agent declared compensable is automatically cache:false, consistently, by the existing mechanism, with no new policy. Wave 1 ships Agent uncached and compensable and does not need the sandbox solved. Promoting Agent to sealed (and therefore cassette-cacheable) is wave 4, gated on the experiment: run an agent inside StepSandbox with a deliberately under-declared read set and confirm the read FAILS rather than succeeding unobserved. Smithers cannot do this — its capture mode is cli-text with traceCompleteness "capture-failed" (AgentTraceCollector.js:429) and its only substitute is one jj commit id over the whole tree (jj.js:113), which over-invalidates on every unrelated edit and guarantees a permanent miss.

=== H. NO `outputs: "discovered"` MODE, EVER ===
Lenses B and C agree and A does not contradict. Target.ts:59-63 is explicit: "an untrusted cache entry must never get to choose which paths are verified, and an implementation must not get to decide after the fact that it produced fewer outputs than it declared." The sandbox-plus-patch design gets the same expressiveness — the patch IS the discovered diff — without weakening the manifest. Where declared outputs are genuinely impossible (claude-auto-update), the substitute is AgentApply's bounded `allow` path list, checked before the write; sota-research.yml:165-176 already hand-writes exactly that as a nine-path `git add --`.

=== I. THE CACHE KEY, FIELD BY FIELD ===
Reuse StepKey.ContentIdentity. No new key format.
 body: prompt TEMPLATE digest (not the rendered string — bindings go in inputs, so a miss is explainable); output-schema STRUCTURAL digest (the schema is both injected into the prompt and the validation predicate, so a hit under a changed schema serves a value the consumer cannot decode); temperature, topP, seed, maxTokens (all of them — temp 0 and temp 1 are different experiments and maxTokens truncates); decode/repair policy; mode (contract|check|refresh); rubric digest. NOT in body: retry count, attempt number, loop iteration (Smithers folds iteration and attempt at engine.js:5804, which is why its loop iteration 2 can never hit iteration 1 even when byte-identical — do not copy), cost/latency budgets, failOn (belongs to the verdict target so a threshold change does not discard the expensive half).
 layers: the existing frozen slots plus (a) resolved model snapshot, not the requested alias, (b) agent harness identity — CLI binary digest or SDK version plus injected-system-prompt digest. The harness slot is the likeliest omission and the most damaging: the built-in Claude skills live inside a 313MB binary that moved twice in two days.
 capabilities: tool SET and tool SCHEMAS. Tool IMPLEMENTATIONS follow the existing rule (a flow-implemented tool contributes its declaration identity; a tool shelling to an external binary is a layer). A SKILL IS A FILE — SKILL.md plus frontmatter is a readSet entry, digested like any other input, needing no new mechanism. Structural consequence: NETWORK CAPABILITY DECIDES CACHEABILITY. A grant of net:* to an arbitrary endpoint means the target reads a world the key does not name -> cache:false mechanically. This is how claude-auto-update.yml (whose whole point is `npm view solc versions --json`) is excluded without a policy note.
 inputs: prompt bindings as InputRef. Ref folds the DIGEST OF THE SETTLED UPSTREAM VALUE, never the upstream's plan key — so in research->plan->implement, editing the research prompt does not invalidate implement when the research output is unchanged. Without this, chained agent targets cascade-invalidate and the cache is worthless past depth one.
 hermetic.readSet: MEASURED digests, re-verified on hit. This is already built and is most of what makes shared replay safe: a measured mismatch journals stale_read_set, evicts under a provenance fence, and falls through to real execution (ActionPersistence.ts:946); an unmeasurable read set refuses the hit for this dispatch but leaves the row alone. readsKeyedExactly (:526-527) refuses cacheability while any read is still a glob, so an agent target declaring Input.Glob context is not shared-cacheable until the scheduler pins it.

=== J. THE DETERMINISM BOUNDARY, AS A TAXONOMY IMPLEMENTERS CAN APPLY ===
Two independent axes, which every survey conflated. Axis A: is the VALUE reproducible (value-reproducible / verdict-stable / distribution-valued)? Axis B: is the point a value or a MUTATION? The catalog already rules on B in prose at PackageJson.ts:1120-1123 — "it is never cache admissible: a hit for a target whose whole purpose is to leave a file behind would report success for a manifest that was never written." That sentence settles every *Land task and every deploy.

Class 0 — pure, misfiled as agentic. scoreTrace.ts; workflow graph render; eval-suite manifest validation; the prefer-smithers hook (stdin JSON -> stdout JSON, no fs, no net, no clock); risk-reviewer's 4-category gate classification; the fallbackAgents authority-carryover audit; workflow/test/UI file pairing; AgentContextParity. Ordinary cacheable targets. SHIP FIRST — cheap, several are security-relevant (the fallbackAgents audit catches silent authority WIDENING).
Class 1 — verdict over content-addressed subject. Review with the mode triad. `check` is cacheable and NEVER calls a model.
Class 2 — distribution-valued. EvalSample (run, cache:false) / EvalScore (test, cache:true, keyed via Input.produced). Honest limit: a soak exists to re-run UNCHANGED inputs; cache:false is necessary but insufficient, and "run again on a schedule though nothing changed" is a scheduler concern, not a key concern.
Class 3 — generative into the tree. Agent (build) -> deterministic verifier (test, Input.produced) -> AgentApply (run, irreversible). Two non-optional constraints: a deterministic validator sits behind every agent proposal (sota-research.ts:12-16 revalidates the model's registry with the generator's own validateRegistry; release.tsx:312-336 has a plain non-agent task read the audit's typed output and throw), and any model answer that must survive between runs lands in a NONHERMETIC field cache keyed on a COARSENED digest, never in the target's own result store.
Class 4 — effectful. run + verbGate + irreversible, never cacheable, bounded allowlist as the verification substitute.
Class 5 — not functions of the workspace. Do not model: checkin/remind-me (input is a lossily-compacted transcript), @claude comment triggers, human approvals (a cached approval is a security defect — the content of the approval is that a person saw THIS diff), prod canaries (value derives from re-running when nothing changed), bench timings and wasm sizes (properties of the machine), .e2e-flakes/history.json (input includes its own prior outputs across unbounded runs — state, not a build step), built-in Claude skills.

=== K. KEY COARSENING, AND ITS HONEST COST ===
The least obvious and most important technique, already implemented at PackageJson.ts:766-772: "The listing, not the source bytes. A package's description does not change because one line of one function did, and re-deriving it on every source edit would turn a cached nonhermetic value into a model call per commit." For a nonhermetic value the key covers the SEMANTIC SURFACE (exported signatures, file listing, schema shapes), not byte content. The anti-pattern is Smithers' jjPointer. THE COST MUST BE NAMED: a coarsened key is deliberately blind to changes it judges irrelevant, so every agentic rule's docstring must state WHAT IT IS CHOOSING NOT TO LOOK AT. That is a real weakening of the cache-correctness guarantee and should be documented as one, not glossed.

=== L. THE ANALOGUE OF "THE REBUILD IS THE GATE" ===
In a deterministic build, regeneration is both the production and the verification, because re-derivation is cheaper than the check it replaces. For agentic work both preconditions fail: re-derivation is expensive AND unreproducible. The move is to invert the direction of trust — THE RECORD IS THE INPUT AND THE VERIFIER IS THE GATE. flows already wrote the argument down at GithubCiGen.ts:837-871: contract mode asserts a PROPERTY (every declared gate still runs) rather than byte equality, which is "strictly weaker than byte equality and the strongest thing you can assert about an artifact you cannot reproduce." That is the correct DEFAULT MODE for every agentic target. A model-written JSDoc block should not be gated on "the model would write this again"; it should be gated on "this block still names every parameter the signature declares" — a property, checkable offline, cacheable, true regardless of which model wrote it.

=== M. RULE SHAPE, CONCRETELY ===
Kinds vocabulary is VERIFIED at Target.ts:31 as ["build","test","lint","run","docs"], verbGate exists at :220, and cache accepts `boolean | ((attrs) => boolean)` at :501 with both function and constant forms already used (GithubCiGen.ts:897, ToolBuild.ts:1074). NOTHING needs to be added to the Target API for any of this. The engine changes actually required are exactly three: (1) Input.Produced plus planner support for keying on a dependency's output manifest — the only substantial one, and the design is UNSOUND without it; (2) widen captureOutputs from `<R>(produced: Node.Node<Exec.Result, Exec.ExecError, R>, ...)` (ToolBuild.ts:1044) to `<A, E, R>` — its body uses neither A nor E, so this is a one-line change that lets Agent, EvalSample and Workflow reuse it verbatim; (3) plan-time attr assertions beyond schema checks, so EvalSample.requireHard and Workflow's sealed-closure scan fail during construction via the existing declarationRejected path that names the BUILD.ts line.

=== N. ONE RECONCILIATION DEFECT TO FIX ===
VERIFIED: packages/plan/src/KeyMaterial.ts:67 has `nondeterministic`; packages/core/src/KeyMaterial.ts's KeyMaterial interface does NOT. The core interface and the plan schema disagree, so a core-planned node cannot declare nondeterminism and would take the strict conflict path — the flagship sealed case tripping the alarm the carve-out was written to silence. Fix before any agentic node is planned through core.

openQuestions.question: Does the D1-D15 sandboxing work actually enforce a declared read set at the syscall boundary for a SPAWNED AGENT CLI, or only for in-process actions?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: This is the single decision that determines whether shared caching of agent targets is achievable at all. flows' admission gate is verified at ActionPersistence.ts:527 as tier==="sealed" && boundaryMode==="hard" && readsKeyedExactly. If a spawned `claude` or `codex` process can read outside its declared set unobserved, no Agent target can honestly be sealed, cassettes are pointless, and Wave 4 collapses to journal-replay-only. Building the cassette machinery first and discovering this second would waste the largest single chunk of work in the plan. Smithers has already proven the negative case: its capture mode is cli-text with traceCompleteness "capture-failed" and its only substitute is one jj commit id over the whole tree.
options: Sandbox covers spawned subprocesses -> Agent ships sealed in Wave 4, cassettes are worth building, the thesis holds fully.

Sandbox is in-process only -> Agent stays compensable forever, shared caching of agent runs is off the table, and the deliverable is the artifact split (Agent->verifier->Apply) with EvalScore and Review-check as the only cacheable agentic halves. The thesis survives in weakened form and should be stated that way in the docs.
Sandbox coverage is unknown -> run the Wave 4.1 experiment BEFORE committing to Wave 3's tier, because tier choice changes the rule's public shape.

openQuestions.question: Is Input.Produced (output-keyed dependency edges) already in scope for D1-D15's cache-by-default and folder-level-units work, or is it net-new?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Everything in this plan is unsound without it, and it is the only substantial engine change proposed. If D1-D15 already delivers output-manifest keying under another name, Wave 0.1 is a rename and the agentic waves start immediately. If it is net-new and D1-D15 made a conflicting choice (e.g. keying consumers on producer plan keys), the two designs collide and the collision must be resolved before either ships. A wrong guess here means either duplicated planner work or an agentic graph that silently replays verdicts about artifacts that no longer exist.
options: Already delivered by D1-D15 -> map names and proceed.
Net-new and compatible -> build as specified in Wave 0.1.
Net-new and conflicting -> escalate; the agentic design cannot be finished until the keying model is settled.

openQuestions.question: Should a model-driven GATE be allowed to fail CI at all, given that the resolved design means `check` mode never calls a model?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: The design's strongest move is PackageJson's rule: check and write never call a model, so a fresh checkout with a cold cache and no model CLI still checks green. Applied to Review, that means CI gates on a COMMITTED findings artifact, not on a live model verdict. That is a real semantic change to the three existing lint/BUILD.ts targets, one of which (durableIdentityGuard) currently fails the build. If the intent is that these remain live gates, Review needs a fourth mode and the 'CI never calls a model' property is given up. Guessing wrong means either building a mode nobody wants or silently downgrading a gate that was meant to be binding.
options: Committed-findings gate (contract/check cacheable, refresh is a run verb) -> CI is offline, deterministic, cacheable; the cost is that a rubric violation is caught at refresh time, not at push time.

Live gate retained as a fourth mode (cache:false, kinds:['lint']) -> keeps push-time enforcement, gives up offline CI, and re-opens the flip-rate question: a gate that flips one run in ten is not a gate, so this option requires measuring verdict stability first.
Both, with durableIdentityGuard live and the two documentation lints on the committed-findings path.

openQuestions.question: Should flows subsume Smithers workflow EXECUTION, or stop at the artifact boundary?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: The plan proposes Workflow as a narrow sealed-batch rule and leaves everything interactive as an Exec target under `run`. The alternative — flows scheduling general Smithers runs — is a much larger project and the surveys give three independent reasons it cannot work (the graph is not known before it runs; a run is a supervised service that needed a caretaker restarting dead engines every three minutes across multi-day runs; approvals cannot be replayed). But the two engines are ALREADY colliding physically: smithers.db is 1.4GB in the flows repo root and .smithers/executions holds 114 entries. If the intent is eventual convergence, the Workflow rule should be designed as a migration path rather than a permanent narrow slice, and the sealed-closure scan becomes a much bigger investment.
options: Artifact boundary only -> Workflow stays narrow, interactive runs stay outside the graph and expose artifacts via Input.produced. Smallest, safest, matches all three lenses.
Convergence -> design Workflow as the first step of absorbing the engine; budget for the closure scan, durable timers, approvals-as-barriers, and a run-results store. Several times the work.
Keep them separate permanently and document the seam, treating Smithers as an external tool the way foundry or cargo is.

openQuestions.question: Extend Runtime with rust/zig/foundry/python, or add a parallel Toolchain declaration?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Runtime.Name is verified as Literals(["node","bun","deno"]) and its semantics are 'the interpreter every tool runs under'. Rust and Zig are not interpreters and Foundry is not a runtime, so widening Runtime may corrupt a clean concept — but a parallel Toolchain duplicates the measure-and-refuse machinery and forces every rule to accept two kinds of toolchain dep. This choice is baked into the attrs of Cargo, ForgeBuild, ZigBuild, NapiBuild and DockerImage simultaneously, so changing it later is a five-rule refactor. It also decides whether browser/workerd/vercel become Runtime names (needed by six smithers CI lanes) or something else again.
options: Widen Runtime.Name to include rust|zig|foundry|python|go|browser|workerd|vercel and accept that 'runtime' now means 'declared, measured host capability'.
Separate Toolchain namespace with the same measure-and-refuse contract; Runtime stays interpreters-only.
Runtime for anything that executes the workspace's own code (node, bun, deno, browser, workerd, vercel), Toolchain for anything that compiles it (rust, zig, foundry, solc).

openQuestions.question: Do the D1-D15 visibility rules constrain what an Agent's `context` globs may reach, and is a cross-package agent context a visibility violation?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Agent's `context` is the enforced read set and it is what makes the key usable — declare it narrowly and you get hits, declare it as the repo and you get Smithers' permanent miss. But a realistic agent task ("raise coverage in packages/engine") legitimately needs to read its dependencies' sources, which under folder-level units plus visibility may be a boundary violation. If visibility forbids it, every Agent needs an explicit escape hatch, and the shape of that hatch (a visibility exemption attr, a Filegroup the dependency exports, or a special agent-context visibility class) has to be decided before Agent's attrs are frozen.
options: Agent context is subject to normal visibility; dependencies must export a Filegroup for agents to read -> most principled, most declaration overhead.
Agent context gets a distinct visibility class ('readable-by-agents') declared on the producing package.
Agent context is exempt from visibility and only the sandbox constrains it -> simplest, but it makes the read set a per-agent decision rather than a package-owner decision.

openQuestions.question: Is a coarsened cache key acceptable as catalog policy, and must every agentic rule document what it declines to look at?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Key coarsening is the technique that makes nonhermetic values economically viable — PackageJson.ts:766-772 keys a description on the file LISTING rather than source bytes, explicitly to avoid a model call per commit. Generalizing it is the difference between a cache that hits and one that does not. But a coarsened key is deliberately blind to changes it judges irrelevant, which is a real weakening of the cache-correctness guarantee that flows otherwise holds absolutely. If the answer is 'no coarsening', the agentic cache is probably not worth building and that should be reported as a finding rather than worked around. If yes, the docstring obligation should be a review rule, not a convention.
options: Allowed, with a mandatory docstring section naming the ignored change class, enforced by a lint over the targets package.
Allowed only for values stored in the nonhermetic field cache, never for a target's own result store (this is what PackageJson does today).
Not allowed -> agentic keys are full-content and the hit rate should be measured before anything else is built, because a near-zero rate kills the economics.

openQuestions.question: Do we need a distinct freshness marker for targets that must re-run on a schedule even though nothing changed, or is that purely a scheduler concern outside the graph?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: cache:false and 'must be resampled even when the key is unchanged' read identically to an operator but mean different things. Soak suites, prod canaries and eval sampling all fall here, and both surveys flagged that a build system which only knows 'cached / not cached' cannot express them. Getting this wrong in either direction is cheap to fix in isolation but expensive to retrofit if EvalSample and Bench ship with the wrong metadata shape, since it changes how CI generation reads the graph.
options: Add Target metadata freshness: 'cached' | 'uncached' | 'resampled' with an optional schedule, and let GithubCiGen emit a cron for resampled targets.
Keep it out of the graph: these are scheduled invocations of run-verb targets, declared in the CI generator's config rather than in the target.
Defer entirely until Wave 5 and ship EvalSample/Bench with cache:false, accepting a later metadata addition.
